lines: They stopped. All six, at once, some time before dawn, and after that they were only bells.
I have been up that tree twice looking for what did it and there is nothing up there to find.
Briarbell slept. Nobody has said one word about that either.
They have stopped. All six, at about two, and the wind is still doing everything it was doing.
A bell does not stop in a wind. There is no way for a bell to stop in a wind.
Half of Briarbell is stood under that tree in the dark waiting for one of them to go. Me as well.
All six. All night. I said tuned bells argue and these ones only talk.
They are arguing. Six hundred times up that tree and I have never heard them do it.
Nobody in Briarbell slept and nobody in Briarbell has said one word about it.
Heard the fourth bell go while you were in there. It only does that for a good one.
That is superstition and I know it is superstition.
I have been up that tree six hundred times and I still believe it.
Six bells. Bronze, and older than the deeds to every house you can see.
My family has kept them since there was a family to keep them.
We do not tune them. Tuned bells argue. These ones just talk.
You BEAT her? Nobody beats her, she's ANCIENT.
...that came out wrong and I'd like it back please.
You're not allowed to climb it. I've climbed it eleven times.
There's a bell up top that you can't see from down here.
It's got writing on it and it isn't in any letters I know.

bb_grocer: Roots, greens, four kinds of bean, and apples that came off the wrong tree.
Not that tree. Nobody eats off that tree.
It fruits, mind. Every autumn. We rake it up and burn it and nobody says why.

lines: Cuttings, seed, and grafting stock from the Glasshouse up the lane.
Ask Ilve about the bell tree cuttings if you want to watch a calm woman go quiet.
Forty years of trying. Not one has taken. Not one.

bb_baker: Bread, and honey off the hives out past the allotments.
The bees work the bell tree and nothing else will touch it.
The honey's dark as a bruise and sweeter than it has any right to be.

lines: So she gave you the Crest and the knife with it. Course she did.
Mind where you cut. Half the thorn in this valley is holding a bank up.
Beds, frames, and the long borders down to the fence. All mine.
Tove keeps the Hall hedge herself. Won't let anyone else near it.
Sixty years of one woman and one hedge learning each other's habits.
Word's out already. It always is.
She'll have gone back to the hedge. She always does. Says it stops her getting proud.
Arch is open, then. That is the easy half.
The hard half does not have a puzzle in it, I'm afraid.
Bell Hall. Verdant and Beast, and the first Crest in Caelora if you can take it.
Word of advice, and I give it to everyone: she does not hit hard.
Work out what that means before you go in, not while you're in there.
They went back through the wood the way they came, and they took four days over it.
My barley is flat where they crossed and I am not putting in a claim for it.
They still went to the tree on the way out. Every last one of them.
They are not coming out of the wood. They are coming through it, from the far side, all day.
Coast kin. Things with fins on, in my barley, forty miles from any water they belong in.
And they still go to the tree. Whatever else has changed, they still go to the tree.
Twelve acres of barley and a fence I'm always mending.
The kin come down out of the wood at dusk and go straight past it. Every night.
They're going to the tree. I stopped asking why about thirty years ago.
Walked down from Stonewake. Two days, and one of them uphill in both directions.
There's a ruin off Route 2 that wasn't marked on my chart.
Stone, and old. I couldn't get in. Door with no handle on it.
I sweep the square. Leaves, mostly. It never runs out of leaves.
My grandmother swept it. Hers did too.
Somebody has swept under that tree every day for longer than the town's had a name.

bb_clinic_child: My Nibbet's asleep. It's not hurt, it just does that.
The lady says that's called being a Nibbet.

lines: Hall week doubles our work and I would not swap it.
Everyone comes in the same door, cheerful. Half of them come back through it quiet.
They all go back a second time. That's the part I like.

bb_shop_regular: I come in for twine and I leave with tonics. Every time.
Harrow could sell rain to a river.
Buy the vessels though. Genuinely. The road north is not empty.

lines: I am going back down to the coast on Thursday. There is a boat with my name written against it.
I could feel it wrong through a hull and now I cannot, and I have been down to check twice.
I hated this room. I am going to be extremely sentimental about this room.
I came inland to stop thinking about the sea and the sea has followed me up a valley.
I said you could feel it wrong through a hull. You can feel it through a floor now.
There is no ship I know of that I would rather be on than in this room, and I hate this room.
Off a coaster out of Tideglass, three weeks inland and I'm still walking odd.
The sea's wrong down there. Flat wrong. You can feel it through the hull.
Come this far up and all anyone worries about is bees. It's restful.
I have measured that tree four times and got four answers.
Rings say nine hundred years. The bells say four hundred. The town says always.
Somebody hung metal in a living thing and the living thing grew around it and kept it.
Forty cuttings off the bell tree. Warmth, water, grafting stock, prayer.
Not one has taken root. Not in forty years, and I am good at this.
It does not want copies. I have come round to finding that admirable.
Splice two plants and one of them has to give way. That is the whole trade.
The one that gives way is usually the stronger. It has more to spare.
Take that how you like. I mean it about pears.
Tove's Crest. Well now.
I'll write to Sorrell tonight. He asked us to send word the moment it happened.
The moment it happened, he wrote. Not IF. He is going to be insufferable.
You're Sorrell's, then. He wrote ahead. Four pages.
Three of them were about currents in the Caeloran and one was about you.
He is a good man and a terrible correspondent.

bb_house_a_child: There's a book about my dad's shelf that Dad won't let anyone borrow.
It's by somebody from Hearthmere. That's where you're from, isn't it?
Dad went quiet when I said that. He does that a lot.

lines: Honey, jam, and three years of both in that cupboard.
Take a jar up to Tove if you're going. She never asks and she always finishes it.
Best window in Briarbell and my aunt keeps the shutters half closed.
Look at the top bell. Go on. The small one, right up in the crown.
It's not bronze. It's never been bronze. Nobody in this town will say what it is.
